a1.say: Let's solve Colliding Rocks, using the Stack approach.

a1.cap: Rocks move along a line. The size is |rocks[i]|; positive moves right, negative moves left, all at the same speed. When two meet, the smaller one shatters (both shatter if equal). Return the rocks that remain, in order.
a1.say: Rocks move along a line. The size is |rocks at i|; positive moves right, negative moves left, all at the same speed. When two meet, the smaller one shatters (both shatter if equal). Return the rocks that remain, in order.

lines: Rocks move along a line. The size is |rocks[i]|; positive moves right, negative moves left, all at the same speed. When two meet, the smaller one shatters (both shatter if equal). Return the rocks that remain, in order.

a1.cap: For example, with rocks = [5,10,-5], the answer is [5,10]. 10 destroys −5.
a1.say: For example, with rocks equals 5, 10, -5, the answer is 5, 10. 10 destroys minus 5.

a1.cap: Survivors wait on a stack. A left-moving rock collides with right-moving rocks on top of the stack: smaller right-movers shatter and are popped; if the top is bigger, the new rock shatters; if equal, both go.
A rock that survives every collision is pushed.
Let's walk through it with rocks = [10,2,-5].
a1.say: Let's walk through it with rocks equals 10, 2, -5.

a1.cap: -5 smashes the smaller rock on top.
Time complexity is O(n) and extra space is O(n).
a1.say: Time complexity is O of n and extra space is O of n.

a1.cap: That's the Stack approach. Now try writing it yourself, in Java or Python!
